requirements: The core contributions of 'Fine-tuning Reinforcement Learning Models is Secretly a Forgetting Mitigation Problem' have been reproduced, demonstrating that vanilla fine-tuning of pre-trained RL models suffers from forgetting of pre-trained capabilities (state coverage gap and imperfect cloning gap) across NetHack, Montezuma's Revenge, and RoboticSequence, and that knowledge retention techniques (EWC, BC, KS, EM) mitigate this problem, including achieving a new neural-model state-of-the-art of over 10K points on NetHack Human Monk.

sub_tasks.requirements: The NetHack Human Monk fine-tuning experiments have been reproduced, showing that vanilla fine-tuning deteriorates while knowledge retention methods (KS, BC, EWC) surpass the prior state-of-the-art, with KS achieving over 10K points, driven by the imperfect cloning gap.

The results show that vanilla fine-tuning on NetHack Human Monk deteriorates relative to the pre-trained policy's performance, consistent with the paper's description of vanilla fine-tuning suffering from the imperfect cloning gap.

The results show that Fine-tuning + BC and Fine-tuning + EWC also surpass the prior neural-model state-of-the-art on NetHack Human Monk, though to a lesser extent than KS, consistent with the paper's description that KS, BC, and EWC all outperform vanilla fine-tuning and the prior state-of-the-art.

The results show that Fine-tuning + EWC surpasses the prior neural-model state-of-the-art average return of approximately 5,000 points on NetHack Human Monk, though achieving a lower average return than Fine-tuning + KS, consistent with Figure 1/3a.

The results show that Fine-tuning + KS achieves a higher average return than both Fine-tuning + BC and Fine-tuning + EWC on NetHack Human Monk, consistent with the paper's description that KS, BC, and EWC all outperform vanilla fine-tuning and the prior state-of-the-art, with KS achieving the largest improvement (over 10K points).

The results show that Fine-tuning + KS (kickstarting) achieves a higher average return than Fine-tuning + BC on NetHack Human Monk throughout the later stages of training, consistent with Figure 1/3a and the paper's statement that KS achieves the largest improvement, exceeding 10K points.

The results show that Fine-tuning + KS (kickstarting) achieves a higher average return than Fine-tuning + BC on NetHack Human Monk throughout the later stages of training, consistent with Figure 1/3a.

The results show that Fine-tuning + KS (kickstarting) achieves a higher average return than Fine-tuning + EWC on NetHack Human Monk throughout the later stages of training, consistent with Figure 1/3a, and that EWC saturates at a comparatively lower value.

The results show that Fine-tuning + KS achieves roughly 2x the average return of the prior neural-model state-of-the-art (approximately 10K points versus the prior ~5K points), matching the paper's explicit statement of a '2x, 10K points when compared to the previous 5K' improvement, and that this margin is larger than the margins achieved by BC or EWC over the same baseline.

The paper's explanation is verified: the improvement of knowledge retention methods over vanilla fine-tuning on NetHack Human Monk is attributed primarily to mitigation of the imperfect cloning gap (rather than the state coverage gap), consistent with the paper's framing of NetHack as a setting dominated by the imperfect cloning gap.

The RoboticSequence (Meta-World) multi-stage fine-tuning experiments have been reproduced, showing that BC, EM, and EWC mitigate the state coverage gap and outperform vanilla fine-tuning and training from scratch, with BC solving all four stages 80% of the time.

The 'hammer' Meta-World sub-task (hammer-v2, hammer in a nail) is configured as the first stage (E_1) in the RoboticSequence, using the standard Meta-World hammer task success condition to determine when the agent advances to the next stage.

The 'push' Meta-World sub-task (push-v2, push an object from one place to another) is configured as the second stage (E_2) in the RoboticSequence, using the standard Meta-World push task success condition to determine when the agent advances to the next stage.

The 'peg-unplug-side' Meta-World sub-task (peg-unplug-side-v2, remove a bolt from a wall) is configured as the third stage (E_3) in the RoboticSequence, using the standard Meta-World peg-unplug-side task success condition to determine when the agent advances to the next stage.

The 'push-wall' Meta-World sub-task (push-wall-v2, push an object around a wall) is configured as the fourth and final stage (E_4) in the RoboticSequence, using the standard Meta-World push-wall task success condition to determine episode completion.

The four sub-tasks are wired together into a single fixed ordering (hammer -> push -> peg-unplug-side -> push-wall) such that the agent must complete each stage in this exact sequence within one episode, with no reordering or skipping of stages permitted.

The environment is implemented such that transitioning between the four sub-tasks (hammer, push, peg-unplug-side, push-wall) occurs within a single continuous episode (i.e., the underlying Meta-World environment/state is swapped or reconfigured for the next stage without resetting the overall episode/step counter across stages), rather than treating each sub-task as an independent episode.

The observation space for RoboticSequence is constructed by concatenating the current robot configuration information (as defined by the underlying Meta-World task, per Yu et al. 2020) with a one-hot encoded vector representing the current stage ID, as described in Appendix B.3.

An episode of RoboticSequence is only considered fully successful if the robot sequentially completes all four sub-tasks (hammer, push, peg-unplug-side, push-wall) within a single episode, matching the paper's statement that 'the robot is successful only if during a single episode it completes sequentially' all four sub-tasks.

The Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) policy and Q-value networks are implemented as 4-hidden-layer MLPs with 256 neurons each and Leaky-ReLU activations, with layer normalization applied after the first layer, and a separate output head per stage selected via the stage ID.

Algorithm 1 (RoboticSequence) is implemented: starting at environment index i=1 and timestep t=1, the agent takes steps in environment E_i using policy π, advancing to the next environment and resetting the timestep counter upon solving E_i, until all N environments are solved or the time limit T is reached, returning the number of solved environments.

Algorithm 1 for RoboticSequence is implemented such that the environment index i is initialized to 1 (i.e., E_1 = hammer, the first stage in the sequence) and the timestep counter t is initialized to 1 at the start of a rollout/episode.

Algorithm 1 is implemented such that at each timestep the agent takes an action sampled from policy π conditioned on the current observation (which includes the stage one-hot ID as per the observation space construction) and executes it in the current sub-environment E_i, receiving the next observation and reward.

Algorithm 1 is implemented such that when the agent solves the current sub-environment E_i (success condition met), the environment index i is incremented to move to the next sub-environment E_{i+1} and the timestep counter t is reset to 1, matching the per-stage advancement logic described in Algorithm 1.

Algorithm 1 is implemented such that the episode/rollout loop terminates when either all N=4 environments (hammer, push, peg-unplug-side, push-wall) have been solved, or the time limit T (200 steps per stage) is reached without the current stage being solved, whichever occurs first.

Algorithm 1 is implemented to return the number of environments solved (an integer between 0 and N=4) as the outcome of the rollout, which is used as the basis for computing the overall RoboticSequence performance metric plotted in Figure 3c.

The environment terminates the episode exactly when the agent succeeds at the current stage or when the time limit (200 steps) is reached, in both cases signaling SAC that the state is terminal (i.e., no bootstrapping of the Q-value target is applied), diverging from the original Meta-World's indefinite-horizon convention.

The four knowledge retention methods used throughout the paper — Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), behavioral cloning replay (BC), kickstarting (KS), and episodic memory (EM) — have been correctly implemented as auxiliary losses/buffers applied to the actor only.

Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is implemented as an auxiliary regularization loss (Eq. 2) applied only to the actor parameters, penalizing squared deviation of current actor parameters from the pre-trained parameters, weighted by the diagonal Fisher Information Matrix computed with respect to the pre-trained policy, scaled by an environment-specific regularization coefficient (2·10^6 for NetHack, per Table 1/3 elsewhere in the rubric).

The diagonal Fisher Information Matrix used in the EWC loss is estimated from the pre-trained policy π* (e.g., via squared gradients of the log-likelihood of actions sampled from π* on pre-training-distribution states), correctly matching the formulation referenced in Section 2/Appendix C.

Behavioral cloning (BC) is implemented as an auxiliary KL-divergence loss (Eq. 3) applied only to the actor, penalizing the KL divergence between the pre-trained policy π* and the current fine-tuned policy π, evaluated on states sampled from a buffer of trajectories collected using π* (the expert/pre-trained model), scaled by an environment-specific coefficient.

A fixed buffer of state-action pairs or trajectories generated by the pre-trained policy π* (or, for Montezuma's Revenge, a separately pre-trained PPO+RND agent achieving ~7000 reward) is constructed prior to fine-tuning and used as the data source for computing the BC auxiliary loss throughout training, matching the environment-specific buffer sizes described elsewhere (e.g., 10,000 pairs for RoboticSequence, >500 trajectories for Montezuma's Revenge).

Kickstarting (KS) is implemented as an auxiliary KL-divergence loss (Eq. 4) applied only to the actor, penalizing the KL divergence between the pre-trained policy π* and the current fine-tuned policy π, evaluated on states visited online by the current fine-tuned policy during training (rather than on a fixed pre-collected buffer), distinguishing it from BC's use of expert-visited states.

The KS auxiliary loss is scaled by a coefficient (0.5 for NetHack) with an exponential decay schedule applied per training step (decay factor 0.99998 for NetHack), progressively reducing the influence of the kickstarting loss as training proceeds, matching the description in Section 4/Appendix C.

Episodic memory (EM) is implemented as a mechanism that pre-populates the off-policy replay buffer (used by SAC) with a fixed set of state-action-reward transitions collected from the pre-trained policy π* on the pre-training-distribution stages, and protects these entries from being overwritten/evicted for the remainder of training, ensuring the policy continues to be trained on them alongside newly collected online transitions.

The implementation correctly restricts episodic memory (EM) to algorithms using an off-policy replay buffer (SAC, used for RoboticSequence), and does not attempt to apply EM to APPO (NetHack) or PPO (Montezuma's Revenge), consistent with the paper's statement that EM cannot be trivially applied to on-policy algorithms.

For all four knowledge retention methods (EWC, BC, KS, EM) across all environments, the auxiliary loss or buffer protection is applied exclusively to the actor/policy network, with the critic/value network trained purely via the standard RL objective (no auxiliary regularization or protected critic-only replay data), consistent with the critic regularization coefficient of 0 specified for RoboticSequence (Table 3) and the general description that knowledge retention targets the actor.

When applying any of EWC, BC, or KS during fine-tuning (as specified for NetHack), the shared encoders are frozen and the entropy bonus is turned off during training, matching the training configuration described for the NetHack knowledge-retention experiments.

Kickstarting (KS) is correctly omitted from the Montezuma's Revenge and RoboticSequence experiments, consistent with the paper's finding that KS fails in state coverage gap settings because it tries to match the pre-trained model's outputs on CLOSE states that were never visited during pre-training.
